question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second and third columns of the matrix $P?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the second and third columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{2}={v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{3} & ={v}_{3}-\frac{{v}_{3}\cdot {e}_{2}}{{e}_{2}\cdot {e}_{2}}{e}_{2} \\  & ={v}_{3}-\frac{1}{5}{e}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{2}$ and ${e}_{3}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the second and third columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{3}}{‖{e}_{3}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{24}{5}}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{15} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
